summary: Describes a way to tell RTP receivers when packets are sent at a time other than their nominal transmission time. It also provides a way for receivers to give better jitter reports that account for those offsets. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a sender mails a packet earlier or later than it should. This adds a note saying so, so the receiver doesn't think the post office is at fault.

questions: rtp jitter reports with timing offsets
what is rtp transmission time offset
how does rtp measure network jitter
what is the toffset rtp header extension
subtitle: A small RTP header extension that tells receivers when a packet was really sent, so source-made timing wobble is not blamed on the network.

tldr.problem: RTP jitter calculations assume each packet is sent at the moment its timestamp says. Traffic smoothing, out-of-order video frames and retransmissions break that assumption, so sender-made delay gets reported as network jitter.
tldr.mechanism: A header extension carries a 24-bit signed transmission offset that, added to the RTP timestamp, gives the effective sending time. A new RTCP packet type, IJ, reports inter-arrival jitter that takes those offsets into account.
tldr.outcome: Receivers and network elements can tell source-introduced timing variation from network jitter. Normal jitter calculations must still ignore the offsets, and only the original source may add them.

today: RFC 5450 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Transmission Time Matters
sections.content:
RFC 3550 bases its network jitter calculations on the presumption that packets are sent essentially in line with their RTP timestamps. That must hold on average over long periods, but not for every single packet.

The RFC lists three cases. Bursty streams, such as video where I-frames are much larger than P or B frames, may need traffic smoothing. Video with forward-decode dependencies may need frames sent in decoding order (sequence number order), so a frame sent early does not match its RTP timestamp. And a retransmitted packet has a different actual sending time than the original even though both share a timestamp.

Knowing the real sending time can help the receiver or intermediate network elements. This RFC adds that information as an RTP header extension. It does not define a transmission timestamp, only the relationship between relative sending times and relative RTP timestamps.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender sometimes sends packets a bit early or late on purpose. Without a note, the receiver sees odd gaps and blames the road. This RFC adds the note.

sections.title: The Transmission Offset
sections.content:
For two packets with timestamps S2 and S1, the classic sending interval is (S2 - S1). With offsets O1 and O2 in each packet, the original sending interval can be deduced as (S2 + O2) - (S1 + O1).

The offset is defined against a recent RTCP sender report that relates RTP timestamp S0 to NTP timestamp N0. A later packet with timestamp S1 is nominally sent at N1 = N0 + RtoN(S1 - S0). If it was actually sent at a different time Na, the offset is O1 = NtoR(Na - N1), converted back to the RTP timescale.

The reported transmission time is T1 = S1 + O1. These values only have meaning when two or more are compared. The point where transmission time is measured is left to the transmitter, though it should be consistent from packet to packet. Any unreported variation added at or after that point is treated by the receiver as network jitter.
sections.plainLanguage: The offset says how much earlier or later than the clock says a packet really left. Add it to the stamp on the packet and you get the real departure time.

sections.title: The Extension Block
sections.content:
The offset travels in-band using the general RTP header extension mechanism of RFC 5285. The payload is a 24-bit signed integer. The block has an ID, a length field len=2 meaning 3 bytes follow, and the transmission offset.

The value is signed because the sign depends on how RTP and NTP times were first mapped. Without scanning a whole stream, you cannot guarantee that mapping keeps every offset positive, so negative values are allowed.

Declaring the extension uses the URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:toffset in an extmap attribute. No extension attributes are defined and no other setup information is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is a tiny number stuck on the packet. It can be positive or negative, like saying five minutes early or five minutes late.

sections.title: A Worked Smoothing Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives a stream with timestamps and sizes of 200 (2 KB), 300 (4 KB), 400 (2 KB) and 500 (12 KB), ending at 600. That is 20 KB over 400 time units, or 1 KB per 20 time units. Traffic smoothing sends the packets at x + 0, x + 40, x + 120 and x + 160, with the end at x + 400.

The choice of x is essentially arbitrary, since only relative values matter. If the first packet is claimed to go out at its own timestamp (offset 0, so x is 200), the offsets are 0, -60, -80 and -140. If x is 400 instead, the offsets are 200, 140, 120 and 60. Both are equally valid.
sections.plainLanguage: If you hand out sweets evenly instead of in clumps, some sweets go out early. The offsets record how early each one went, and any starting point works.

sections.title: Rules for Senders and Networks
sections.content:
When the extension is in effect for a stream, it MAY be left out of packets whose offset is 0. An untagged packet then has an implied offset of 0 if the extension is in effect, and an unknown offset if it is not.

An RTP client MUST NOT use the offsets in its normal jitter calculation. The sender or analysing network elements cannot always know whether the offsets were taken into account, so that calculation keeps using raw reception times.

The extension is defined only for the source to report. Intermediate nodes that are not the source MUST NOT add it or change an existing value. A network element that terminates an RTP flow and starts a new one as the source may add the extension to the new flow.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the sender may write the note. Anyone passing the packet along must leave it alone, and the receiver's normal timing check ignores it.

sections.title: Extended Jitter Reports
sections.content:
The jitter from Section 6.4.1 of RFC 3550 includes any source-introduced jitter. To report the actual network jitter, the RFC defines a new RTCP packet type, IJ, with packet type 195. It holds one inter-arrival jitter value per report.

The packet must follow a receiver report inside a compound RTCP packet and MUST have the same RC (reception report count) as that report. Each value uses the same formula as sender and receiver reports but with T = S + O in place of S, so D(i,j) = (Rj - Ri) - ((Sj + Oj) - (Si + Oi)). If a stream has no offset information, the value equals the one in the receiver report.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra report says how bumpy the road really was after subtracting the bumps the sender made itself.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The offsets are only informative, and the RFC finds it hard to see security issues in attaching them to media streams. The security considerations of RFC 3550 still apply.

Malicious senders or systems tampering in transit could send implausible offsets that confuse the receiver or produce misleading jitter values. Both sides should take care that this does not cause denial of service or other problems.

IANA registered RTCP packet type 195 (IJ, extended inter-arrival jitter report) and the extension URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:toffset in the RTP Parameters registry.
sections.plainLanguage: A cheater could write silly notes on packets, so receivers should not trust them blindly.

fields.name: ID
fields.desc: Extension identifier from the RFC 5285 mechanism.

fields.name: Transmission Offset
fields.desc: Signed offset added to the RTP timestamp.

fields.name: RC
fields.desc: Same as the receiver report's reception report count.

fields.name: inter-arrival jitter
fields.desc: One value per report, repeated RC times.
